content: The nasal mucous membrane is a specialized tissue that lines the nasal cavities and is closely attached to the underlying periosteum or perichondrium. It is continuous with the skin at the nostrils (nares) and with the mucous membrane of the nasopharynx through the posterior nasal apertures, also known as choanae. Additionally, it connects to the conjunctiva via the nasolacrimal and lacrimal ducts, and to the frontal, ethmoidal, sphenoidal, and maxillary sinuses through various openings in the nasal meatuses. The mucous membrane is thickest and most vascular over the nasal conchae, particularly the middle and inferior conchae, and is also relatively thick over the nasal septum. However, it becomes very thin in the meatuses, on the floor of the nasal cavities, and within the sinuses. This tissue is one of the most frequently infected areas in both adults and children. Inflammation of the nasal mucosa can lead to significant disruption of daily activities, with symptoms such as nasal congestion, headaches, and mouth breathing. The thickness of the mucous membrane narrows the nasal cavities, making the middle and inferior nasal conchae appear larger and more prominent than they do in the skeletal structure. Furthermore, the openings that communicate with the meatuses are considerably reduced in size. The structure of the nasal mucous membrane varies depending on its location and function. In the respiratory region, the epithelium is columnar and ciliated, with goblet cells interspersed among the columnar cells. Smaller pyramidal cells are located at the base of the epithelium. Beneath the epithelial layer lies a fibrous layer infiltrated with lymphocytes, forming diffuse adenoid tissue in many areas. Below this is a nearly continuous layer of glands, both mucous and serous, whose ducts open onto the surface of the mucosa. In the olfactory region, the mucous membrane has a yellowish color, and the epithelial cells are columnar but non-ciliated. These cells are of two types: supporting cells and olfactory cells. Supporting cells contain oval nuclei located in their deeper parts, forming a zone of oval nuclei. The superficial portion of each supporting cell is columnar and contains yellow pigment granules, while the deeper portion extends as a delicate process that branches and communicates with similar processes from neighboring cells, forming a network within the mucosa. Interspersed among the deep processes of the supporting cells are bipolar nerve cells, known as olfactory cells. Each olfactory cell consists of a small amount of granular protoplasm with a large spherical nucleus and has two processes: a superficial process that extends between the columnar epithelial cells and projects onto the mucosal surface as a fine, hair-like structure called the olfactory hair, and a deep process that extends inward, often beaded, and continues as the axon of an olfactory nerve fiber. Beneath the epithelium and extending through the thickness of the mucous membrane is a layer of tubular, often branched glands known as Bowman’s glands. These glands are structurally similar to serous glands. The nasal mucous membrane is commonly affected during viral infections such as the common cold and influenza, leading to inflammation and associated symptoms.
